children: A pronounced inverse correlation has emerged over the past seven months, with McDonald's
stock tumbling precisely as the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield
has climbed 32% since early March, while McDonald's

stock has dropped an identical 32% over the same timeframe. The recent divergence is even more concentrated, as yields jumped 14% by rising on 19 of the last 23 trading days; simultaneously, MCD fell 14% by dropping on 19 of those last 23 days.
is climbing as the Federal Reserve embarks on an interest-rate hiking cycle as inflation proves persistent, which inherently pressures dividend-paying "bond proxies" like McDonald's
. The company has a 3.3% forward yield, trailing the US10Y's ~5.2%, so its
is becoming less attractive to income investors as risk-free Treasury yields surge.

Meanwhile, the fast-food giant is buckling under fundamental headwinds, including meager U.S. same-store sales and a cautious outlook from CEO Chris Kempczinski, who recently warned that flat industry traffic and accelerating inflation are the new normal.
